metadata.author: Alex Philippidis

content.value:
Six months after Sanofi’s new CEO committed the pharma giant to replenishing its pipeline—notably in respiratory drugs—Belén Garijo took her biggest step toward fulfilling that goal, announcing plans today to acquire Insmed for $41 billion, in what would be the year’s largest merger-and-acquisition (M&A) deal.

In announcing the deal overnight, Sanofi declared that the transaction was intended to broaden its presence in respiratory diseases—a key therapeutic area of Insmed along with immunology and inflammation, neuro, and rare disease drugs. Sanofi also termed the deal “a compelling strategic fit, building on Sanofi’s longstanding experience in immunology and rare diseases.”

“Insmed builds on our already successful presence in respiratory diseases through its highly differentiated portfolio, strong science and proven commercial success,” Garijo said in the statement. “Together, we have the opportunity to build on these achievements, reach more patients globally and reinforce our leadership in diseases of significant unmet medical need.”

“This acquisition is a major strategic step to significantly accelerate our mid- and long-term growth trajectory and further strengthen our mid- and early-stage pipeline,” Garijo added.

Garijo reinforced that message during a conference call with analysts this morning to discuss the planned Insmed buyout. The CEO said acquiring Insmed was intended to help recoup an estimated €8 billion ($8.752 billion) in revenue that Sanofi expects to lose between 2031-2035, the first four years after its aging blockbuster drug Dupixent® (dupilumab), co-marketed with Regeneron Pharmaceuticals, loses key patent exclusivity.

Dupixent generated a total $17.419 billion in Q1-Q3 global net product sales this year, up 35% from $12.867 billion in January-September 2025. Sanofi reports all revenue from Dupixent but splits profits 50-50 with Regeneron globally.

‘Continue to be bullish’

“We continue to be bullish on Sanofi’s acquisition of INSM following today’s call, which reinforced the Dupixent patent cliff offset rationale,” David Risinger, a senior managing director and senior research analyst covering diversified biopharmaceuticals at Leerink Partners, wrote this morning in a research note.

Based in Bridgewater, NJ, Insmed has successfully developed and now markets two FDA-approved respiratory treatments. One is Brinsupri ® (brensocatib), which won FDA approval last year as the first drug authorized to treat non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis (NCFB). The other is Arikayce® (amikacin liposome inhalation suspension), which won agency authorization in 2018 as a treatment for mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) lung disease.

Insmed’s pipeline is led by a potential third respiratory treatment, the late-stage candidate Treprostinil Palmitil Inhalation Powder (TPIP), a prostanoid which is in Phase III studies for three indications: Pulmonary hypertension associated with interstitial lung disease (PH-ILD); pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH); and progressive pulmonary fibrosis (PPF). TPIP is also in Phase II development for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF).

In September, the FDA accepted under Priority Review Insmed’s application for Arikayce for the treatment of MAC lung disease as part of a combination antibacterial drug regimen. The agency set a target decision date of January 28, 2027, under the Prescription Drug User Fee Act (PDUFA).

Sanofi reasons that TPIP could become a significant growth driver—indeed a blockbuster for Sanofi beyond 2030, subject to successful clinical development, regulatory approvals, and commercial execution.

Brinsupri accounted for nearly three-fourths (73%) or $917.1 million of the $1.256 billion in total revenue reported by Insmed for the first three quarters of this year, 29% above the second quarter and more than 32 times the $28.1 million generated in Q3 2025. Total revenue during Q1−Q3 2026 is more than triple (267%) above the $342.6 million garnered during January−September 2025.

Sanofi reported even higher Q1-Q3 revenue for Brinsupri in its announcement of the deal, stating that the drug delivered $1.09 billion in revenue through September 30, 2026, “with substantial additional growth expected.” The discrepancy was not immediately explained.

Insmed earlier this month raised the low end of its full-year revenue guidance range to investors on Brinsupri to $1.35 billion from $1.25 billion, keeping the high end at $1.4 billion. Those numbers are well above the company’s initial 2026 Brinsupri revenue forecast of at least $1 billion.

Arikayce generated $338.8 million during Q1−Q3 2026, up 8% from $314.5 million a year earlier, with revenue guidance also raised at the low end to $460 million from $450 million, while the company has maintained the high end at $470 million.

Capping speculation

Sanofi’s announcement caps a week of speculation by investors triggered by a Bloomberg News report that cited unnamed sources in reporting that Sanofi was weighing whether to acquire Insmed, in a potential blockbuster transaction.

The news touched off a buying spree that sent Insmed’s stock price on Nasdaq soaring 24% from $119.80 on November 18, the day before the published report surfaced, to $149.09 yesterday. Shares climbed another 14% this morning on Sanofi’s confirmation of the deal, trading at $170.26 as of 11:54 am ET after opening slightly higher at $170.49 90 minutes earlier.

Sanofi’s full ordinary shares on Euronext Paris jumped 9.8% from €85.26 ($92.96) to €93.58 ($101.96) as of 11:37 am ET, while its American depositary shares on Nasdaq rose nearly 10% this morning as of 11:53 am ET from $46.77 to $51.29.

“We are not surprised to see a strategic recognize the unique combination of strong commercial potential + low clinical risk across the INSM portfolio,” Faisal Khurshid, a managing director and equity research analyst with Jefferies, wrote this morning in a research note. “The deal price is above our $165 PT [price target] and seems fair. On synergy and rationale we think this makes sense.”

GEN ‘takeover target’

At $175 per share, Sanofi’s deal price for Insmed marks a 17.5% premium to Insmed’s closing price yesterday and a 46% premium from the company’s stock price the day before news reports centered on Sanofi as its potential buyer.

Insmed was among companies highlighted by GEN last year in its A-List of Top 10 Takeover Targets of 2025, after analyst Andrea Newkirk, PhD, vice president, biotechnology equity research with Goldman Sachs, concluded that the company could make an attractive buyout target for larger biopharmas focused on treating respiratory diseases.

And while Insmed was forecasting at the time that Brinsupri would generate peak year sales of at least $5 billion for bronchiectasis alone, Newkirk projected a higher sales figure of $5.9 billion, which she concluded “likely significantly” underestimated the drug’s true potential.

Sanofi does not expect its acquisition of Insmed to have any impact on its financial guidance for 2026. The pharma giant upgraded its guidance to investors when it reported Q3 earnings last month, revising its sales growth forecast to a low-teens percentage at constant exchange rates (CER), up from the 10% predicted after Q2 and the high single-digit percentage at CER projected after Q1. Business earnings per share at CER is now expected to grow by a mid-teens percentage, up from earlier guidance of “slightly faster than sales.”

Sanofi said the transaction is expected to add to its business earnings per share (EPS) by the end of 2028. The company said it was funding the acquisition through a combination of debt financing and cash on hand, and had secured committed financing in support of the transaction.

The boards of Sanofi and Insmed have approved the transaction, which is still subject to approval by Insmed shareholders, receipt of U.S. and non-U.S. regulatory approvals, and other customary conditions. Subject to the satisfaction or waiver of these conditions, Sanofi said, the transaction is expected to close in the first half of 2027.

“This acquisition is another example of how we are executing on our strategic roadmap with momentum to drive Sanofi’s next phase of growth,” Garijo added.
